blocks.text: The figure of the eagle upon its throne, and the council of the birds sitting around it. That is, in the assembly of the birds the eagle is painted, marked out by a crown and raised high on a throne, and the other birds stand by it. And of the eagle Baal Hatturim, at the very beginning of this chapter, says: הוא מלך העופות, It holds kingship over the birds. Finally, the Fathers define this very thing in the same way. Thus Ambrose, Hexaëm. book 5, ch. 18, calls the eagle a royal bird and assigns it royal eminence. Jerome on Mich. 1: The eagle, which is queen of the birds. And on Dan. VII.: As the lion among the beasts, so the eagle holds kingship among the birds. Epiphanius in the Physiologus, chapter 6: Ἔστι γὰρ ὁ ἀετὸς βασιλεὺς τῶν ὀρνέων· [Esti gar ho aetos basileus tōn orneōn] For the eagle is king of the birds, or queen, if you prefer. Theodoret, in the Preface to the Canticle, on the passage Ezech. XVII, 3.: Ἀετὸν μὲν τὸν βασιλέα (ἐνόησεν), ἐπειδὰν καὶ τὸ ζῶον βασιλικόν· [Aeton men ton basilea (enoēsen), epeidan kai to zōon basilikon] By the name of eagle he meant the king, because it is a royal animal. Theodore of Heraclea on Psal. CII.: Ἐπειδὴ ὁ ἀετὸς δοκεῖ βασιλεύειν τῶν πετεινῶν ἁπάντων· [Epeidē ho aetos dokei basileuein tōn peteinōn hapantōn] Because the eagle seems to rule over all the birds. And shortly after: Διὰ γὰρ τοῦ ὄρνιθος τοῦ ἀετοῦ τὴν βασιλείαν αἰνίττεται [Dia gar tou ornithos tou aetou tēn basileian ainittetai], For by the eagle he signifies the kingdom. What of the fact that it was commonly believed that the eagle is at war with the wren because the latter καλεῖται πρέσβυς, καὶ βασιλεὺς [kaleitai presbys, kai basileus], is called senator and king, as though the eagle begrudged it this name? So the Philosopher testifies, Hist. book 9, ch. 11. Hence Pliny, book 10, ch. 74: Eagles and the wren are at odds, if we believe it, because the wren is called king of the birds.

Where the eagle, in Hebrew נשר neser, gets its name has so far escaped the teachers. For the fancy of Rabbi Bechai on Gen. II., that it derives from the Chaldee נשר nesar, which means to fall down, is absurd: the reason given is that, when it has soared in flight up to the element of fire, as they indeed claim, it then falls headlong into the sea. Nor do I agree with those who assert that it is named from the shedding of its feathers, because for the Rabbis נשר means to fall off. Nor with those who derive it from sight, because נשר neser seems to allude to the verb שור sur, which means to see. I most approve of the Arabs, for whom نسر [nasara] nasara means to pluck with the beak, and منسر [minsar] minsar means beak, properly that of a bird of prey. From this, then, they hold that the eagle is called نسر [nasr] nesr, لانه ينسر الشي ويقتلعه [li-annahu yansiru al-shayʾ wa-yaqtaliʿuhu] because it tears and plucks a thing with its beak. So Giauhari, Damir and Alcamus. Other birds of prey also pluck with the beak, to be sure; yet this is attributed by special right to the prince of the birds of prey, the eagle, [col. 165] because its beak is more hooked and it tears more strongly with it. Likewise, to swoop upon prey is common to all of them, which in Hebrew is העיט. Hence עיט ajit is in general [II, 743] a bird of prey. Yet usage among the Greeks made ἀετὸν [aeton] or αἰετὸν [aieton], derived from it, the proper name of the eagle ^{(1)}.

The eagle is remarkable for its talons as well as for its beak; it has them not straight, like a man, but curved and hooked like a lion's. For of the animals that have claws, τὰ μέν εἰσιν εὐθυόνυχα, ὥσπερ ἄνθρωπος· τὰ δὲ γαμψώνυχα, ὥσπερ καὶ τῶν πεζῶν λέων, καὶ τῶν πτηνῶν αἰετὸς [ta men eisin euthyonycha, hōsper anthrōpos; ta de gampsōnycha, hōsper kai tōn pezōn leōn, kai tōn ptēnōn aietos], some have straight claws, like man; others hooked ones, like the lion among land animals and the eagle among birds. So the Philosopher, Hist. book 3, ch. 9. In birds, that is, the talons imitate the shape of the beak. Suidas: Γαμψώνυχα ὅσα τῶν ζώων τὴν ἐπιρυγχίδα γεγάμψωκεν ὑπὸ τὴν γένυν, οἷα ἐστὶν ἀετός· [Gampsōnycha hosa tōn zōōn tēn epirynchida gegampsōken hypo tēn genyn, hoia estin aetos] All animals that have the beak curved under the jaws have hooked talons; of this kind is the eagle. The Grammarians are unsure to which of the two it refers that the eagle which the sleepless Penelope saw is called

For to some ἀγκυλοχείλης [ankylocheilēs] is ὁ ἔχων ἀγκύλα χείλη, ἤτοι τὸ ῥάμφος [ho echōn ankyla cheilē, ētoi to rhamphos], one that has curved lips, [II, 744] that is, a curved beak; to others, ἐπικαμπεῖς τὰς χηλὰς ἔχων [epikampeis tas chēlas echōn], one that has bent claws. In this sense Cleon is called in Aristophanes' Knights
because, like an eagle, he had hooked or rapacious claws, as not only the Scholiast but also Aristophanes himself interprets it. And in Plautus' Pseudolus the cook says,
Do you expect to find any cook Without kite's or eagle's claws?
